summary: This lecture covers three events in the Prophet's youth. First, the Fijar War, which began from a killing in a sacred month and lasted four years, when he was 15 to 19 and gathered arrows, until it ended with blood money. Second, the Hilf al-Fudul pact at Abdullah ibn Jud'an's house after a Yemeni trader was cheated by Al-As ibn Wail; the Prophet SAW and Abu Bakr were the two young men who joined, and he later said he preferred it to red camels. Third, he was offered the management of Khadijah's trade, brought back double the profit from Sham with Maisarah, and Khadijah was drawn to his honesty, with the proposal to be told next week.
keyPoints: The Fijar War began from a killing in a sacred month and lasted four years, and the 15-year-old Prophet SAW gathered arrows.
The war ended when Quraysh paid blood money, because it was ruining trade and Hajj.
Hilf al-Fudul was made to defend the oppressed, and the 20-year-old Prophet SAW and 18-year-old Abu Bakr were the two young men who joined.
The Prophet SAW later said he preferred that pact to red camels.
Khadijah offered him management of her trade because of his honesty, and he brought back double the profit from Sham.

chapters.title: Opening and recap
chapters.summary: The ustaz notes this is lecture 8 and recalls that the Prophet SAW is now 15, a Form 3 age.

chapters.title: The Fijar War begins
chapters.summary: Fijar means wicked. Two traders, Urwah and Al-Barrad, competed to take goods to Ukaz market and Al-Barrad killed Urwah.

chapters.title: The sacred month and the sacred land
chapters.summary: The killing happened in a sacred month, and when Quraysh fled to the Haram they were pursued, violating the sacred land.

chapters.title: A war lasting four years
chapters.summary: The war drew in whole tribes and dragged on for four years over a quarrel between two men.

chapters.title: The Prophet SAW takes part
chapters.summary: He disliked this war but defended the sacred land, and his task was to gather arrows for his uncles.

chapters.title: The war ends with blood money
chapters.summary: Sensible people saw that the war was costing Hajj and trade, and Quraysh paid blood money.

chapters.title: The Prophet's lesson about war
chapters.summary: He grew up hearing the glory of war but later avoided it as much as possible unless attacked.

chapters.title: The Yemeni trader and Al-As ibn Wail
chapters.summary: A Zubaidi man from Yemen sold goods to Al-As ibn Wail, payment due after Hajj, but was put off with 'tomorrow'.

chapters.title: No one helps the weak
chapters.summary: Quraysh refused to help the outsider because Al-As was a big man and one of their own.

chapters.title: Appealing on the hill by the Kaaba
chapters.summary: The man announced his plight from a hill near the Kaaba, and Zubair ibn Abdul Muttalib heard him.

chapters.title: Abdullah ibn Jud'an and the gathering
chapters.summary: Abdullah ibn Jud'an gathered the leaders, and only two young men came: the Prophet SAW and Abu Bakr.

chapters.title: The Hilf al-Fudul pact
chapters.summary: They pledged not to let the weak be wronged even by their own, and wiped perfume on the Kaaba's cloth.

chapters.title: The debt is claimed
chapters.summary: They knocked on Al-As ibn Wail's door and made him pay, and the Yemeni man went home happy.

chapters.title: Better than red camels
chapters.summary: Years later the Prophet SAW said he would prefer being called to such a pact over red camels, and the ustaz explains helping the oppressed.

chapters.title: Khadijah offers work
chapters.summary: Khadijah, a rich trader with 700 camels, heard of Muhammad's honesty from her sister Hala and offered him the role of manager.

chapters.title: Maisarah, profit and Khadijah's interest
chapters.summary: With Maisarah he brought back double the profit and returned early, and Khadijah, twice married before, was drawn to him.

dalil.translation: The Prophet SAW said that if he were called again to a pact like Hilf al-Fudul, he would prefer it to red camels.
dalil.context: The ustaz relates the Prophet's words about the pact when he was already a messenger. He does not name a narrator or source.

books.context: A sirah summary covering the Fijar War, Hilf al-Fudul and the marriage to Khadijah.

people.context: Offered a lower price to take goods to Ukaz market and was killed by Al-Barrad.

people.role: The Quraysh trader who killed Urwah
people.context: Angry at losing the job, he killed Urwah in a sacred month.
Refused to pay the Yemeni trader until forced after Hilf al-Fudul. Father of Amr ibn al-As.
The son of Al-As ibn Wail who would conquer Egypt.
Cheated, he appealed to the Quraysh, which led to the pact.
Heard the trader's appeal and went to Abdullah ibn Jud'an.
Gathered the tribal leaders at his house to make Hilf al-Fudul.
With the Prophet SAW, one of the two young men who joined the pact.
Advised him to accept Khadijah's offer as a good deal.
Owned 700 camels, offered Muhammad the management of her trade and was eventually drawn to him.
Ran a sheep business that employed Muhammad and told Khadijah of his honesty.
Accompanied the Prophet SAW to Sham and wrote reports, impressed by his honesty.
A child from Khadijah's first husband.

people.role: A trader who wanted to marry Khadijah
people.context: Turned down by Khadijah because of his character.

people.context: Turned down by Khadijah because of his character.

sirah.era: The Prophet's youth to early adulthood (15 to 25)
sirah.summary: This lecture covers the Fijar War, Hilf al-Fudul, his work with Khadijah and Khadijah's interest in him.

lessons.title: Do not fight over small matters
lessons.body: A four-year war began from a quarrel between two men that could have been settled.

lessons.title: Respecting the sacred months and land
lessons.body: Killing in a sacred month and attacking the sacred land were considered grave wrongs.

lessons.title: Settling with blood money
lessons.body: Compensation ended the war and saved trade and Hajj.

lessons.title: Avoiding war unless attacked
lessons.body: The Prophet SAW later minimised wars and fought only when attacked.

lessons.title: Defending the weak
lessons.body: The pact pledged not to let the weak be wronged.

lessons.title: Fairness even towards one's own group
lessons.body: They promised to correct a wrongdoer even if he belonged to their group.

lessons.title: Upholding justice for all
lessons.body: Muslims help the wronged even of another religion and do not mistreat animals.

lessons.title: Honesty opens the door to provision
lessons.body: Because he was honest he was offered a big job without applying.

lessons.title: Trustworthiness at work
lessons.body: He did not cheat or slack off even when no one was watching.

lessons.title: Finishing work and returning promptly
lessons.body: He did not party in Sham but packed up and returned.

glossary.meaning: Meaning wickedness, the name of the war because it was fought in a sacred month.
A great market where the Arabs held trading fairs.
An Arab clan or tribe fiercely loyal to its own.
Months in which fighting was forbidden among the Arabs.
Blood money paid for someone killed, for example 100 camels.
A pact to defend the oppressed.
The costliest and rarest camel, a symbol of great wealth.
A business partnership: one brings capital, the other works, and profit is shared.
